summary:
**Ana & The Moon Crew** is a free, interactive 3D educational web game designed to inspire children aged 7–12 to explore space science and lunar engineering. Players join Ana and her crew through seven hands-on learning chapters covering solar power, radiation protection, life support, lunar habitats, rovers, communication, and food and water management. They then apply their knowledge in Survival Mode, taking on the role of Base Commander to manage resources, make critical engineering decisions, and protect their crew during realistic lunar emergencies.

What makes the project unique is its integration of real NASA scientific datasets, including solar storm records, radiation measurements, and astronaut health research, transforming authentic space science into engaging, evidence-based gameplay. By combining storytelling, 3D simulations, engineering challenges, and interactive decision-making, the project makes complex aerospace concepts accessible to young learners. It aims to nurture STEM curiosity, develop engineering problem-solving skills, and inspire the next generation of space explorers, particularly among children in Sarawak and beyond.
details:
What it does
Ana & The Moon Crew is a free 3D web game that trains children aged 7 to 12 as junior astronauts at a Moon base. It has two modes:

  • Learning Mode: 7 Academy chapters: Solar Power, Radiation Shelter, Life Support, Lunar Habitat, Dust and Rovers, Communication, and Food and Water. Each chapter has a story, a guide character, hands-on activities, an engineering challenge, a quiz and badges. Children balance oxygen and CO₂, build habitat layers, plan a robot rover’s route around craters, aim an antenna to call Grandma on Earth, and grow a space salad. Players who finish all seven chapters type their name onto a Junior Lunar Engineer certificate.
  • Survival Mode: the child becomes Base Commander and makes crew decisions turn by turn during emergencies.

How NASA data makes it real
Survival Mission 2 replays the real X5.1 solar flare of 11 November 2025:

  • It uses event records from NASA’s DONKI database for the flare, the CME, the solar energetic particle event and the geomagnetic storm.
  • Every turn uses the real hourly GOES proton levels. Children must get the crew to the shelter before the protons arrive, which in real life was 16 minutes after the flare peaked.
  • The debrief plots the real proton curve with the child’s own decisions marked on it.
  • It also uses ISS radiation readings from NASA’s OSDR RadLab to compare a solar storm in Earth orbit with one on the Moon.

Mission 3 draws on NASA OSDR studies of muscle and bone loss in space to teach the trade-off between exercising and saving air. Chapter 07 uses the Canadian Space Agency’s food production toolkit.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Children learn real space engineering and space science by doing, not just reading.
  • Failure is kind: Mission Control sends help and a tip to try again, so children build confidence rather than fear.
  • The whole game runs from one HTML file, works offline and needs no installation. It suits schools in Sarawak and other areas with slow or limited internet.
  • Teachers can unlock every mission for classroom use.
  • My goal is to bring real NASA science to rural and urban classrooms in Sarawak and beyond, and to inspire the next generation of space engineers.

Tools and technology

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • three.js for the 3D Moon base, characters and scenes.
  • SVG charts drawn from embedded data snapshots.
  • Data from NASA DONKI, GOES (via DONKI), NASA OSDR and RadLab, and the CSA food production toolkit.
  • Atkinson Hyperlegible, an easy-read font, for accessibility.
  • Playwright for automated play-testing on desktop and mobile.
  • AI assistance (Claude) for coding support and drafting.

Creativity
Most space games either teach facts or simulate missions. This one connects the two:

  • Children first learn each system hands-on, then must apply it under pressure in a real event, replayed from real data.
  • The debrief turns their own choices into a data story: “this is what really happened, and this is where you were.”
  • Story elements such as a birthday call to Grandma make the science personal and memorable.

Factors I considered

  • Age-appropriate design: big buttons, hints, short text and an easy-read font.
  • It must work on phones and low-cost devices, with or without internet.
  • Scientific accuracy, with every alert and chart crediting its NASA source.
  • Gentle handling of failure.
  • Room to grow, with a Bahasa Malaysia version, more missions, live “space weather today” data and a teacher guide for Sarawak schools planned next.
